source_text: Τρεπτὸν δὲ ἀτρέπτου ὄντος τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐκ ἂν εἴη ὅμοιον· ὥσπερ οὐδὲ τὸ κτισθὲν τοῦ κτίσαντος. Διὰ τοῦτο περὶ μὲν ἡμῶν σκοπῶν ὁ ἅγιος ἔλε γεν· Ὁ Θεὸς, τίς ὁμοιωθήσεταί σοι; καὶ, Τίς ὅμοιός σοι ἐν θεοῖς, Κύριε; θεοὺς λέγων, τοὺς κτισθέντας μὲν, μετόχους δὲ γενομένους τοῦ Λόγου, ὡς αὐτὸς εἶπεν· Εἰ ἐκείνους θεοὺς εἶπε, πρὸς οὓς ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐγένετο. Τὰ δὲ μετέχοντα οὐκ ἂν εἴη τὰ αὐτὰ οὐδὲ ὅμοια τοῦ μετεχομένου. Περὶ ἑαυτοῦ γοῦν ἔλεγεν· Ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ Πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν, ὡς τῶν γενητῶν μὴ ὄντων οὕτως. Ἐπεὶ ἀποκρινάσθωσαν οἱ τὴν Ἀρίμηνον προτείνοντες, εἰ κτιστὴ οὐσία δύναται εἰπεῖν· Ἃ βλέπω τὸν Πατέρα ποιοῦντα, ταῦτα κἀγὼ ποιῶ. Ποιούμενα γάρ ἐστι τὰ γενητὰ, καὶ οὐ ποιοῦντα· εἰ δὲ μή γε, καὶ ἑαυτὰ ἐποί ησαν. Ἀμέλει εἰ, ὡς λέγουσι, κτίσμα ἐστὶν ὁ Υἱὸς, καὶ ποιεῖ αὐτὸν ὁ Πατὴρ, πάντως ἂν ἐποίησε καὶ ἑαυ τὸν ὁ Υἱὸς, δυνάμενος ποιεῖν ἃ ποιεῖ ὁ Πατὴρ, ὡς εἶπεν αὐτός· ἀλλ' ἄτοπον καὶ λίαν ἀσύστατόν ἐστι τὸ τοιοῦτον· ποιεῖν γὰρ ἑαυτὸν οὐδεὶς δύναται. Πάλιν δὲ εἰπάτωσαν, εἰ δύναται τὰ γενητὰ εἰπεῖν· Πάντα, ὅσα ἔχει ὁ Πατὴρ, ἐμά ἐστιν; Ἔχει δὲ τὸ κτίζειν, τὸ δημιουργεῖν, τὸ ἀΐδιον, τὸ εἶναι παντοκράτωρ, τὸ ἄτρεπτον. Τὰ δὲ γενητὰ οὐ δύναται ἔχειν τὸ δημιουργεῖν· κτιστὰ γάρ ἐστιν· οὐδὲ τὸ ἀΐδιον· ἀρχὴν γὰρ ἔχει τοῦ εἶναι· οὐδὲ τὸ παντοκράτωρ καὶ ἄτρεπτον· κρατούμενα γὰρ καὶ τρεπτῆς φύσεώς ἐστιν, ὥσπερ αἱ Γραφαὶ λέγουσιν. Οὐκοῦν εἰ ταῦτα τοῦ Υἱοῦ ἐστιν, οὐκ ἐξ ἀρετῆς, ὡς εἴπομεν, ἀλλὰ τῆς οὐσίας αὐτοῦ ἐστι δηλονότι, ὡς εἶπεν ἡ σύνοδος· οὐκ ἐξ ἄλλης οὐσίας ἐστὶν, ἀλλὰ τῆς τοῦ Πατρὸς, ἧς ἐστι καὶ ταῦτα ἴδια· τὸ δὲ τῆς τοῦ Πατρὸς οὐσίας ἴδιον, καὶ ἐξ αὐτῆς γέννημα, τί ἂν εἴη, ἢ πῶς ἄν τις ὀνομάσειεν αὐτὸ, ἢ ὁμοούσιον; ἃ γὰρ βλέπει τις ἐν τῷ Πατρὶ, ταῦτα βλέπει καὶ ἐν τῷ Υἱῷ· Υἱῷ δὲ οὐκ ἐκ μετουσίας, ἀλλὰ κατ' οὐσίαν. Καὶ τοῦτό ἐστιν· Ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ Πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν, καὶ, Ὁ ἐμὲ ἑωρακὼς ἑώρακε τὸν Πατέρα. Ἄλλως τε καὶ ἐκ τούτου πάλιν καλὸν δεικνύναι τὴν ἀφροσύνην αὐτῶν· εἰ ἐξ ἀρετῆς ἕπεται τὸ θέλειν καὶ τὸ μὴ θέλειν, καὶ τρόπων βελτίωσις, ὅμοιος καθ' ὑμᾶς ὁ Υἱός ἐστι τῷ Πατρί· ταῦτα δὲ ποιότητος ἴδια· δηλονότι σύνθετον τὸν Θεὸν ἐκ ποιότητος καὶ οὐσίας λέγετε. Καὶ τίς ὑμῶν ἀνέξεται ταῦτα λεγόντων· οὐ γὰρ σύνθετος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ τὰ πάντα εἰς τὸ εἶναι συντεθεικὼς, οὐδὲ τοιοῦτος, οἷά ἐστι τὰ παρ' αὐτοῦ διὰ τοῦ Λόγου γενόμενα, μὴ γένοιτο! Ἁπλῆ γάρ ἐστιν οὐσία, ἐν ᾗ οὐκ ἔνι ποιότης, οὐδὲ, ὡς εἶπεν ὁ Ἰάκωβος, Παραλλαγή τις ἢ τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα. Οὐκοῦν εἰ δείκνυται οὐκ ἐξ ἀρετῆς· οὐ γὰρ ποιότης ἐν τῷ Θεῷ, οὔτε ἐν τῷ Υἱῷ· δηλονότι τῆς οὐσίας ἴδιος ἂν εἴη· καὶ τοῦτο πάντως ὁμολογήσετε, εἰ μὴ τέλεον τὸ νοεῖν ἀπώλετο ἐν ὑμῖν.
thought_title: The Son is like the Father by substance, not by virtue
orientation: Athanasius continues his argument against the Arians, showing from Scripture and reason that the Son's likeness to the Father belongs to his substance, not to acquired virtue.
pass_a_gloss: But a changeable thing would not be like the unchangeable God; just as neither would the created thing be like the one who created it. For this reason, considering about us, the holy one said: 'O God, who will be likened to you?' and, 'Who is like you among gods, O Lord?' calling gods those who were created, but became partakers of the Word, as he himself said: 'If he called those gods, to whom the Word of God came.' But the things that partake would not be the same as nor like the thing partaken of. About himself, at any rate, he said: 'I and the Father are one,' as created things not being so. Since let those who put forward Ariminum answer, if a created substance can say: 'What I see the Father doing, these things I also do.' For created things are things being made, and not things making; but if not, they also made themselves. Certainly if, as they say, the Son is a creature, and the Father makes him, the Son would altogether have made also himself, being able to make what the Father makes, as he himself said; but such a thing is absurd and utterly untenable; for no one can make himself. Again let them say, if created things can say: 'All things, as many as the Father has, are mine'? But he has the creating, the fashioning, the eternal, the being almighty, the unchangeable. But created things cannot have the fashioning; for they are created; nor the eternal; for they have a beginning of being; nor the almighty and unchangeable; for they are ruled and are of changeable nature, as the Scriptures say. Therefore if these things are the Son's, not from virtue, as we said, but from his substance it is clearly, as the council said: he is not from another substance, but from the Father's, of which these things also are proper; but what is proper to the Father's substance, and offspring from it, what would it be, or how would anyone name it, except consubstantial? For what things one sees in the Father, these things one sees also in the Son; but in the Son not from participation, but according to substance. And this is: 'I and the Father are one,' and, 'The one who has seen me has seen the Father.' Besides, from this again it is good to show their foolishness: if from virtue follows the willing and the not willing, and improvement of ways, the Son is like the Father according to you; but these things are proper to quality; clearly you say that God is composite from quality and substance. And who of you will endure those saying these things? For God is not composite, the one who has put together all things into being, nor such as are the things that came into being from him through the Word—may it not be! For the substance is simple, in which there is no quality, nor, as James said, 'any variation or shadow of turning.' Therefore if it is shown not from virtue—for there is no quality in God, nor in the Son—clearly he would be proper to the substance; and this you will altogether confess, unless the thinking has utterly perished in you.

Fixed glossary term for the underlying being of God.

pass_b_english: But a changeable thing cannot be like the unchangeable God, any more than a created thing can be like its creator. That is why the holy man, considering our condition, said, 'O God, who will be made like you?' (Psalm 82:2 (83:2)), and, 'Who is like you among the gods, O Lord?' (Exodus 15:11). He calls 'gods' those who were created but became partakers of the Word, as the Lord himself said: 'If he called them gods to whom the Word of God came' (John 10:35). But things that partake cannot be the same as, or like, the thing they partake of. About himself, then, he said, 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), because created things are not like that.

So let those who put forward Ariminum answer this: can a created substance say, 'Whatever I see the Father doing, these things I also do' (John 5:19)? For created things are made, and do not make; otherwise they would have made themselves. Indeed, if, as they say, the Son is a creature and the Father makes him, then the Son would certainly have made himself too, since he is able to do what the Father does, as he himself said. But such a thing is absurd and utterly incoherent, for no one can make himself.

Again, let them say whether created things can say, 'All things that the Father has are mine' (John 16:15). The Father has the creating, the fashioning, the eternal, the being almighty, the unchangeable. But created things cannot have the fashioning, for they are created; nor the eternal, for they have a beginning of being; nor the almighty and unchangeable, for they are ruled and of a changeable nature, as the Scriptures say. Therefore, if these things belong to the Son, they are his not from virtue, as we said, but clearly from his substance, as the council said: he is not from another substance, but from the Father's, whose own these things also are. And what belongs to the Father's substance, and is offspring from it—what could it be, or how could anyone name it, except consubstantial? For what one sees in the Father, one sees also in the Son; and in the Son not by participation, but according to substance. And this is what 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30) means, and 'Whoever has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9).

Besides this, it is good to show their folly from another point as well. If likeness follows from virtue, from willing and not willing, and from improvement of character, then according to you the Son is like the Father. But these things belong to quality. Clearly, then, you are saying that God is composite, made of quality and substance. And who will put up with you saying these things? For God, who composed all things into being, is not composite, nor is he like the things that came into being through the Word—may it never be! His substance is simple, in which there is no quality, nor, as James said, 'any variation or shadow of turning' (James 1:17). Therefore, if it is shown that the Son's likeness is not from virtue—for there is no quality in God, nor in the Son—then clearly he belongs to the substance. And this you will certainly confess, unless understanding has utterly perished in you.
